title: Retrospective study to evaluate prognostic factors (especially the importance of resection distance) in the surgical treatment of sarcomas of the extremities and trunk.Clinical parameters, disease extent based on staging examinations (CT, MRI), histology and course (progression, survival) are recorded based on the latest available examination data.
summary:
The prognosis of malignant bone and soft tissue tumours has undergone a decisive change in recent decades. Whereas in 1970 the 5-year survival rate for osteosarcoma, for example, was still below 20%, today approx. 70% of mostly adolescent patients survive [1]. In the discussion about surgical principles and in particular resection limits, a development from amputation to complex limb-preserving and reconstructive procedures can be observed. This is currently successful in approx. 90% of all malignant primary bone tumours with possible limitations to the oncological outcome, which must be discussed with the patient (data from the COSS study: local recurrence after amputation 3.2%, after limb-preserving surgery 7.5%) [2]. Therapeutic approaches with pre- or postoperative chemotherapy or radiotherapy as well as the expansion of diagnostic and surgical options lead to a differentiated surgical approach [3].
The establishment of MRI and, today, PET-CT/MRI has resulted in the opportunity to define the tumour boundaries and thus the extent of resection in a much more differentiated way than was previously possible and justifiable. 
Historically, compartment resection has long been the most established method of adequate tumour resection, especially for soft tissue sarcomas. However, as early as the 1980s and then definitely in the 1990s, this was replaced by wide or compartmentalised resection. 
There are hardly any comparative studies on the differentiation of a wide resection margin. In the case of soft tissue sarcomas, the study by Sadoski from 1993 should be mentioned here [4]. He found no difference in 132 patients with regard to the question of local recurrence in R0 resections  1 mm and > 1 mm. McKee also found no significant differences in overall survival between < 1 mm, 1-9 mm and  10 mm for free resection margins [5]. In 84 sarcoma resections in our own clinic in a recent 12-month period, 8 (9.5%) patients had to be amputated. If 4 patients with planned R1 resection for atypical lipomas are excluded, 8/80 (10%) patients underwent unplanned R1 resection. In the other 72 R0 resections, the resection margin in the very carefully analysed specimens was <1 mm in 31% of cases, between 1-5 mm in 29%, between 5 and 10 mm in 11% and greater than 10 mm in only 29%. In recent years, we have observed an ever smaller safety zone around the tumour. In a recent study from Bochum, this led to the statement that the safety margin would be sufficient as long as there was no ink on the tumour used to stain the outside of the specimen[6].
The aim of this study is therefore to evaluate the safety margin of surgical resection in relation to the occurrence of local recurrence and/or systemic progression of the disease, in addition to the previously known prognostic factors such as tumour type, grading, metastatic status, etc.
conditions: Malignant neoplasm of other connective and soft tissue

interventions.name: All patients with sarcomas of the musculoskeletal system with surgical intervention in the study clinic. All relevant clinical and technical examinations (MRI, CT) carried out as part of routine treatment are included in the study at the time they are performed.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All patients with soft tissue sarcoma of the extremities or trunk who underwent resection at the study hospital.
Exclusion criteria:
None
